content: Ophthalmia neonatorum, also known as neonatal conjunctivitis, is a type of conjunctivitis that occurs in newborns and is typically acquired during delivery. This condition arises when the newborn's eyes are exposed to infectious agents while passing through the birth canal of a mother infected with Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, or herpes simplex virus (HSV). Other potential causes include exposure to bacteria, viruses, or chemical irritants, such as silver nitrate, though the latter is now rarely used. Gonococcal conjunctivitis, caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, typically presents within the first five days of life and is characterized by significant bilateral purulent discharge. In contrast, conjunctivitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis usually manifests after the third day of life and can occur up to two weeks postpartum. Infants with chlamydial infections may later develop pneumonitis between two weeks and 19 weeks of age. Herpetic keratoconjunctivitis, a rare cause of neonatal conjunctivitis, generally occurs within the first two weeks of life. If untreated, HSV conjunctivitis can lead to corneal scarring, ulceration, and even encephalitis due to disseminated infection. Prompt diagnosis is critical to initiate appropriate treatment and prevent severe complications. Laboratory investigations for neonatal conjunctivitis may include Gram staining, cultures, Giemsa staining, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of conjunctival scrapings. Empiric antibiotic treatment often involves erythromycin ophthalmic ointment and ceftriaxone administered intravenously or intramuscularly. Systemic treatment is necessary in cases of chlamydial or HSV conjunctivitis to prevent systemic complications. Pregnant women should be educated on the importance of regular screening and treatment for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) to reduce the risk of neonatal conjunctivitis. Historically, in 1881, Carl Crede introduced 2% silver nitrate as a prophylactic measure against neonatal conjunctivitis. However, silver nitrate is no longer widely used due to its potential to cause chemical conjunctivitis. Ophthalmia neonatorum can be classified based on its etiology into bacterial, viral, or chemical causes. The pathogenesis involves transmission of infectious agents to the newborn via the birth canal, transmembrane infection, or transplacental routes. Chemical conjunctivitis, often caused by silver nitrate, can also occur but is self-limiting and resolves within a few days. Gross pathological findings in neonatal conjunctivitis include conjunctival injection, mucopurulent or non-purulent discharge, pseudomembrane formation, chemosis, and eyelid edema. Microscopic histopathological analysis may reveal stromal infiltration by polymorphonuclear leukocytes, plasma cells, mast cells, and lymphocytes, with numerous neutrophils in bacterial conjunctivitis. The most common bacterial causes of neonatal conjunctivitis include Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Enterobacter species. Viral causes include herpes simplex virus. Chemical conjunctivitis is typically associated with silver nitrate exposure. Differential diagnoses for neonatal conjunctivitis include dacryocystitis, congenital glaucoma, nasolacrimal duct obstruction, preseptal/orbital cellulitis, and keratitis. Globally, ophthalmia neonatorum continues to cause blindness in approximately 10,000 infants annually. The incidence does not vary by gender. In developed countries, the prevalence has significantly decreased due to the discontinuation of silver nitrate prophylaxis. Current prevalence rates in developed countries range from 0.3 to 5 cases per 1,000 live births. In the United States, chlamydial conjunctivitis occurs in 5–60 cases per 1,000 live births, while in the United Kingdom, the rate is approximately 4 cases per 1,000 live births. In contrast, the incidence remains high in many African countries. Risk factors for neonatal conjunctivitis include maternal infections, HIV-positive mothers, premature rupture of membranes, inadequate ocular prophylaxis, ocular trauma during delivery, mechanical ventilation, prematurity, poor prenatal care, and unhygienic delivery conditions. Routine screening for ophthalmia neonatorum is not recommended. However, antibiotic ointments or eye drops are administered to all newborns immediately after birth to prevent conjunctivitis and other infections. This prophylaxis may occasionally cause mild chemical conjunctivitis, which is self-limiting. Screening pregnant women for STIs is recommended to prevent transmission to the newborn. Neonatal conjunctivitis is one of the most common infections in the first month of life. Without adequate prophylaxis, 30–42% of infants born vaginally to infected mothers develop gonococcal conjunctivitis, which typically presents between 2–7 days after birth. This form of conjunctivitis is more severe than other causes and can lead to corneal ulceration, opacification, perforation, blindness, sepsis, or death if untreated. Chlamydial conjunctivitis has a later onset, with an incubation period of 5–14 days, and affects 30–50% of infants born to infected mothers. If untreated, it can progress to purulent discharge, corneal opacification, and blindness. Herpetic conjunctivitis, though rare, can cause corneal scarring, ulceration, and central nervous system involvement if untreated. Pseudomonal conjunctivitis, another rare cause, can lead to severe complications such as corneal perforation and endophthalmitis. Complications of neonatal conjunctivitis include ocular issues such as pseudomembrane formation, corneal edema, thickened palpebral conjunctiva, peripheral pannus formation, corneal opacification, staphyloma, corneal perforation, endophthalmitis, and blindness. Systemic complications of chlamydial conjunctivitis include pneumonia, otitis, and pharyngeal or rectal colonization. Gonococcal conjunctivitis can lead to arthritis, meningitis, anorectal infection, septicemia, and death. Herpetic keratoconjunctivitis can result in encephalitis. Early detection and treatment of neonatal conjunctivitis are associated with a good prognosis. A detailed maternal history, including STI history, ocular prophylaxis at birth, and the timing of symptoms, is essential for prompt diagnosis and management. Laboratory studies for neonatal conjunctivitis include Gram staining, cultures (blood agar, chocolate agar, or Thayer-Martin), Giemsa staining, and PCR. Specific tests for chlamydial conjunctivitis include culture of epithelial cells, Gram staining, Giemsa staining, PCR, DNA hybridization assays, and enzyme immunoassays. For gonococcal conjunctivitis, Gram staining and cultures on chocolate agar or Thayer-Martin media are used. Viral conjunctivitis is diagnosed using viral culture, direct fluorescent antibody testing, and PCR. Imaging studies are not typically required for neonatal conjunctivitis but may be helpful in diagnosing complications such as orbital cellulitis, meningitis, encephalitis, or pneumonia. Treatment of neonatal conjunctivitis involves empiric antibiotic therapy with erythromycin ophthalmic ointment and ceftriaxone. Systemic treatment is necessary for chlamydial and HSV conjunctivitis to prevent systemic complications. Prompt treatment of gonococcal conjunctivitis is essential to prevent corneal ulceration. Systemic acyclovir is required for HSV conjunctivitis to reduce the risk of systemic infection. Corticosteroids should be avoided. Chemical conjunctivitis resolves spontaneously within 2–3 days and does not require treatment. Surgical intervention is not recommended for neonatal conjunctivitis.
